Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: Epidemiology & Risk Factors in GI Cancers
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
This section covers who develops these four gastrointestinal cancers, and why. Each has a distinct typical patient, distinct causes, and a very different prognosis depending on how early it is caught. Recognizing these patterns is what lets a clinician connect a vague symptom like "trouble swallowing" or "blood in the stool" to the right diagnosis before it is too late.

Esophageal Cancer

Esophageal cancer typically presents in the sixth and seventh decades of life, with a lifetime risk of roughly 0.5% in both men and women. It has two biologically distinct histologies that behave almost like two different diseases sharing an organ: squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and adenocarcinoma (ACA). Globally, SCC accounts for about 90% of cases and tends to arise in the upper and middle esophagus, where squamous epithelium normally lives. In North America and Western Europe, however, adenocarcinoma has become dominant (~70% of cases), arising in the distal esophagus from glandular epithelium that has replaced the normal squamous lining, a process called Barrett's esophagus.

Because the two histologies have different causes, it helps to learn their risk factors as two separate mnemonics:

  • SCC, "ABCDEF": Achalasia, Bad diet (high fat, high-temperature foods), Caustic stricture (lye ingestion), Cigarette smoking, Dysplasia/diverticuli, Esophageal webs (Plummer-Vinson syndrome), Familial/genetic.
  • Adenocarcinoma, "BOG": Barrett's esophagus, Obesity, GERD. The relationship with reflux is dose-dependent, weekly GERD symptoms raise risk about 5-fold, and daily symptoms about 7-fold, which is part of why chronic reflux deserves real clinical attention rather than being dismissed as a nuisance.

This histologic split matters far beyond epidemiology: as you will see in later sections, SCC and ACA respond differently to chemoradiation and are staged with separate group-stage tables even though the underlying TNM criteria are identical.

Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma

Pancreatic cancer is disproportionately lethal for how "common" it is, it is only the 11th most common cancer but the 4th leading cause of cancer death, a mismatch explained entirely by how late it is usually caught. Average age at diagnosis is in the 60s, with higher incidence in men and in Black patients. Roughly half of all patients present with distant metastatic disease at diagnosis, because the pancreas sits deep in the retroperitoneum and early tumors rarely cause symptoms. Overall 5-year survival is only about 13%, but that number hides a huge range depending on stage at diagnosis: about 44% for localized disease, 16% for locoregional disease, and only 3% for metastatic disease, which is exactly why resectability (covered later) is the single most important prognostic branch point.

Modifiable risk factors include chronic pancreatitis, cigarette smoking, heavy alcohol use, chronic diabetes, high BMI, red meat intake, and occupational exposures (hydrocarbons, pesticides, heavy metals). A smaller but important group of patients carry hereditary syndromes: hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1/SPINK1), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11/LKB1), FAMMM syndrome (CDKN2A/TP16), Lynch syndrome/HNPCC (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), ataxia telangiectasia, and BRCA1/2 carriers with an affected first-degree relative. These patients are eligible for high-risk screening (EUS and/or MRI/MRCP roughly annually), typically starting at age 40–45 or 10 years before the youngest affected relative's diagnosis.

Clinical Pearl A patient with new-onset diabetes plus unexplained weight loss in their 60s should raise suspicion for pancreatic cancer, the tumor can cause paraneoplastic insulin resistance or destroy islet cells well before it causes pain or jaundice.

Rectal Cancer

Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer and the third most common cause of cancer death in both men and women, with a lifetime risk around 4–5%; rectal cancer specifically accounts for about 40% of all colorectal cancer. Notably, incidence has been rising in younger adults over the last decade, which is why average-risk screening (colonoscopy being the gold standard, every 10 years) now begins at age 45 rather than 50. Patients with a first-degree relative with colorectal cancer, personal history of inflammatory bowel disease, prior pelvic radiation, or prior chemotherapy all warrant earlier and more frequent screening.

Two hereditary syndromes deserve special attention. Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) arises from mismatch-repair gene mutations (most often MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2), produces microsatellite instability, and raises risk not just for colorectal cancer but also endometrial, ovarian, gastric, small bowel, hepatobiliary, brain, renal pelvis, and ureteral cancers, screening colonoscopy starts as early as age 20–25. Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant APC gene mutation that causes hundreds to thousands of colonic polyps, with variants including Gardner syndrome (desmoid tumors, osteomas) and Turcot syndrome (brain tumors); these patients typically undergo prophylactic colectomy once polyps appear.

Anal Cancer

Anal cancer is far less common than rectal cancer, rectal cancer is roughly 5 times more common: with a lifetime risk of about 1 in 500 and average age at diagnosis in the 60s. It is about twice as likely to affect women. The defining epidemiologic fact about anal cancer is that it is, in the great majority of cases, a virally-driven disease: HPV is associated with 85–90% of cases (HPV-16 being the most common subtype), which is why it shares risk factors with other HPV-driven cancers. Additional risk factors include HIV infection, immunosuppression more broadly, smoking, receptive anal intercourse, and a personal history of other HPV-related cancers (cervical, vulvar, or vaginal).

The encouraging epidemiologic fact is that anal cancer most often presents as local or locoregional disease, and, as you'll see in the treatment sections, this is a cancer with unusually high cure rates for a solid tumor, largely because it responds so well to concurrent chemoradiation.

Clinical Pearl Do not confuse anal cancer with rectal cancer just because they are anatomic neighbors. Anal cancer is usually HPV-driven squamous cell carcinoma treated primarily with definitive chemoradiation (surgery reserved for salvage), while rectal cancer is usually adenocarcinoma in which surgery remains the central curative step. They are managed as entirely separate diseases.

Workup & Staging.title: Workup & Staging Fundamentals
Workup & Staging.html:
Before any treatment decision can be made, a cancer must be characterized in two related but distinct ways: how far has it spread anatomically (stage), and can it physically be removed with surgery (resectability). For esophageal, rectal, and anal cancer, stage is the main driver of treatment. For pancreatic cancer, resectability status often matters more than the TNM stage number itself. Across all four cancers, a thorough workup combines history and physical, labs, endoscopic biopsy, cross-sectional and functional imaging, and increasingly, molecular/genomic testing that can change the treatment plan entirely.

Esophageal Cancer

Workup includes a full history and physical, basic labs, a barium swallow study, and upper endoscopy with biopsy, the endoscopist records the distance from the incisors, tumor length, and circumferential extent, all of which matter for radiation planning later. Staging imaging includes CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with oral and IV contrast, FDG PET-CT, and endoscopic ultrasound (EUS), discussed in depth in the Imaging section. Bronchoscopy is added for tumors above the carina to rule out a tracheoesophageal fistula before starting treatment. All patients should be tested for MSI/dMMR status, and patients with locally advanced, recurrent, or metastatic disease should additionally be tested for PD-L1 and HER2, these results directly determine which systemic therapy options (including immunotherapy) are on the table.

T-stage is defined by depth of invasion through the esophageal wall: T1a invades the lamina propria or muscularis mucosa, T1b the submucosa, T2 the muscularis propria, T3 the adventitia, T4a invades the pleura, pericardium, azygos vein, diaphragm, or peritoneum, and T4b invades unresectable structures like the aorta, vertebral body, or airway. N-stage is defined by the number of involved nodes (N1 = 1–2, N2 = 3–6, N3 = ≥7), a system that echoes pancreatic cancer's node-count approach and contrasts with rectal and anal cancer's morphology- or location-based nodal staging. Although T and N criteria are identical for SCC and adenocarcinoma, AJCC v8 uses separate overall-stage-group tables for the two histologies, so the same T/N combination can land in a different stage group depending on histology.

Tumors near the gastroesophageal junction get their own classification, the Siewert system: Type I tumors are centered 1–5 cm above the true GEJ, Type II straddle it (1 cm above to 2 cm below), and Type III are centered 2–5 cm below it. Regional nodal drainage also differs by tumor location, cervical tumors drain to supraclavicular and cervical nodes, mid/lower esophageal tumors to peri-esophageal and subcarinal nodes, and GEJ tumors to left gastric and celiac nodes, which is why the elective nodal volumes covered during radiation differ depending on where the primary tumor sits.

Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma

Workup begins with labs including CA 19-9, then dedicated imaging: CT with a specialized pancreatic protocol (detailed in the Imaging section), MRI abdomen/pelvis, and CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to exclude distant disease. PET-CT is controversial here, it does not replace a dedicated pancreatic-protocol CT and has no clearly defined role beyond occasionally detecting unsuspected metastases. Tissue diagnosis is usually obtained by EUS-guided FNA, ERCP, or CT guidance; importantly, biopsy is not strictly required before surgery if imaging clearly shows resectable disease, but it is required before starting neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Germline genetic testing is required once the diagnosis is confirmed (ATM, BRCA1/2, CDKN2A, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, STK11, TP53), and somatic/molecular testing is pursued for actionable alterations (fusions in ALK/NRG1/NTRK/ROS1/FGFR2/RET; mutations in BRAF/BRCA1/2/KRAS/PALB2; HER2 amplification; MSI/dMMR; tumor mutational burden).

AJCC v8 T-stage is based on tumor size: T1 ≤2 cm (subdivided T1a ≤0.5 cm, T1b 0.5–1 cm, T1c 1–2 cm), T2 >2–4 cm, T3 >4 cm, and T4 = tumor involving the celiac axis, SMA, and/or common hepatic artery: notice that T4 is defined by an anatomic relationship to major arteries, not just size, because that relationship is what actually determines operability. N1 is 1–3 positive nodes and N2 is ≥4. In practice, however, the treatment-defining question for pancreatic cancer is not the AJCC stage group but the separate resectability classification (resectable / borderline resectable / unresectable), based on the precise degree of tumor contact with the SMA, celiac axis, common hepatic artery, SMV, and portal vein, this is covered in detail in the Imaging section, since it is fundamentally a CT-based determination.

Rectal Cancer

Workup centers on a careful digital rectal exam (DRE) with proctoscopy, this remains the single most accurate way to measure a tumor's distance from the anal verge, a number that drives both surgical planning (can the sphincter be spared?) and radiation field design. Labs include CEA (a baseline for later surveillance), and colonoscopy with biopsy establishes the histologic diagnosis; MSI/MMR testing is recommended for all patients given its major treatment implications. Staging imaging pairs CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (to exclude distant metastases) with MRI of the rectum with contrast, which is the standard for locoregional (T and N) staging and is discussed at length in the Imaging section. Patients presenting with obstruction or fistula from a very locally advanced tumor need bowel diversion (colostomy) before neoadjuvant treatment can begin.

AJCC 8th edition T-stage follows depth of invasion through the bowel wall: T1 invades the submucosa, T2 the muscularis propria, T3 the pericolorectal fat, T4a the visceral peritoneum, and T4b adjacent organs or structures. N-stage is more nuanced than in esophageal or pancreatic cancer: N1a is 1 involved node, N1b is 2–3 nodes, and N1c denotes tumor deposits: discrete tumor nodules in the pericolorectal fat with no residual identifiable lymph node, which still upstages the patient even though no actual node is involved. N2a is 4–6 nodes and N2b is ≥7. An important pattern-of-spread pearl: while the liver is the most common metastatic site for both colon and rectal cancer (tumor cells draining via the portal system), rectal cancer, especially mid and low tumors, has a higher rate of lung metastasis than colon cancer, because those tumors drain via the internal iliac nodes into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver's portal filter entirely.

Anal Cancer

Workup for anal cancer has some unique elements reflecting its HPV/HIV-associated biology: a full history and physical with DRE (assessing tumor extent and sphincter function), a gynecologic exam with cervical cancer screening for female patients (given shared HPV etiology), and a discussion of fertility preservation when appropriate. Labs include CBC, CMP, CEA, and, notably, HIV testing (with CD4 count if positive), since HIV status affects both risk assessment and treatment tolerance. Diagnosis requires anoscopy with biopsy of the primary tumor (with HPV testing) plus excisional biopsy or FNA of any suspicious nodes, along with sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy. Staging imaging includes CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, MRI pelvis with contrast, and PET-CT (especially for T3–T4 or node-positive disease), PET-CT's outsized role here is covered in the Imaging section.

Under AJCC 9th edition (2022), T-stage is based on tumor diameter: T1 ≤2 cm, T2 2–5 cm, T3 >5 cm, and T4 invades adjacent organs such as the vagina, urethra, or bladder. N-stage, unlike the node-counting systems used in esophageal and pancreatic cancer, is defined by nodal location: N1a includes inguinal, mesorectal, superior rectal, internal iliac, or obturator nodes; N1b is external iliac node involvement; and N1c is both N1a- and N1b-type involvement together.

Clinical Pearl MSI-H/dMMR testing is now essentially universal across GI oncology, it is recommended for all esophageal and all rectal cancer patients, and is part of standard molecular workup for pancreatic cancer. This single test can redirect a patient from cytotoxic chemoradiation toward checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy alone, so it should never be skipped.
Clinical Pearl For pancreatic cancer, do not equate a low AJCC stage number with an easy surgery. A small tumor that happens to wrap more than 180° around the SMA is, by definition, unresectable regardless of its T-stage, resectability is a separate, largely imaging-based judgment covered in the next section.

Imaging.title: Imaging Across GI Cancers
Imaging.html:
Imaging in radiation oncology answers two very different questions depending on the moment you ask it: first, during staging, "how far has this cancer spread and can it be removed surgically?", and later, during planning, "exactly where does the beam need to go?" Each of these four GI cancers leans on one workhorse modality for its single most decision-critical question, and that is the thread running through this section.

Esophageal Cancer, Endoscopic Ultrasound for T-Stage

CT with oral and IV contrast is useful for detecting distant metastases and gross local invasion (wall thickening greater than 5 mm, periesophageal fat stranding), but it is a poor tool for precise T-staging because it cannot resolve the individual layers of the esophageal wall. FDG PET-CT is the opposite: it is excellent for finding nodal and distant metastatic disease, including normal-sized but FDG-avid lymph nodes that CT alone would call negative, but its sensitivity and specificity for esophageal cancer overall are only around 50% and 80% respectively, and it is poor at depth-of-invasion assessment.

That leaves endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) as the most accurate modality for T-stage, because it can resolve five alternating hyperechoic/hypoechoic layers of the esophageal wall and show precisely how deep a tumor has invaded. EUS T-staging sensitivity is 82–92% for distinguishing higher-stage from T1 disease, with specificity of 97–99%. EUS is also the best modality for regional nodal staging, sensitivity around 85%, rising to 97% when combined with FNA of suspicious nodes (hypoechoic, round, sharp-bordered nodes ≥1 cm without visible intranodal vessels are the features that raise suspicion). In practice, PET-CT and EUS are complementary: PET-CT for distant disease and node detection, EUS for T-stage and node confirmation/biopsy.

Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma, CT Protocol, the Double-Duct Sign, and Resectability

Pancreatic cancer relies on a dedicated pancreatic-protocol CT, acquired at multiple timepoints after contrast injection because tumor conspicuity and vascular detail each peak at a different moment: the early arterial phase (15–25 seconds) best shows arterial anatomy, the delayed arterial/pancreatic phase (30–40 seconds) gives optimal visualization of the pancreas and tumor, the tumor is typically hypodense relative to the avidly enhancing normal gland, and the venous phase (65–70 seconds) is used to assess the portal vein and liver for metastases. A tumor that is obvious on the pancreatic phase can become isodense and nearly invisible on the venous phase alone, which is exactly why a single-phase abdominal CT is inadequate for pancreatic cancer workup.

One classic and highly specific imaging finding is the double duct sign: simultaneous dilation of both the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct. This occurs because a mass in the pancreatic head sits at the anatomic crossroads where both ducts converge at the Ampulla of Vater, a single obstructing lesion can therefore back up both drainage systems at once. This finding is highly concerning for malignancy and should be approached as cancer until proven otherwise, whether identified on CT or on MRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography), a T2-weighted MR technique that directly visualizes fluid within the ducts.

Beyond detecting the tumor, pancreatic-protocol CT answers the question that most determines treatment: is this tumor resectable? That determination is made not from tumor size or TNM stage but from the precise degree of contact between the tumor and the major peripancreatic vessels.

Arterial (SMA, celiac axis, CHA)Venous (SMV, portal vein)
ResectableNo tumor contactNo contact, or ≤180° contact without contour irregularity
Borderline resectable≤180° contact (varies by exact vessel/location)>180° contact, or ≤180° with contour irregularity/thrombosis but a reconstructable vessel segment
Unresectable>180° contact with SMA or celiac axis, or aortic involvementComplete occlusion not amenable to reconstruction

CT has an excellent 89–100% positive predictive value for unresectability using these criteria. Anatomically, roughly two-thirds of tumors arise in the head/uncinate process and one-third in the body/tail, a distinction that matters because head tumors are more likely to cause obstructive jaundice and produce the double-duct sign early, while body/tail tumors often grow silently and present later, closer to the celiac axis and splenic vessels.

Rectal Cancer, Pelvic MRI, the Mesorectal Fascia, and EMVI

MRI of the rectum is the standard for locoregional (T and N) staging, with T2-weighted sequences doing most of the work and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) adding sensitivity for restricted diffusion within tumor. One important limitation: MRI cannot reliably distinguish T1 from T2 disease (that distinction requires EUS), but it substages T3 tumors by how far they extend beyond the muscularis propria into the mesorectal fat, T3a less than 1 mm, T3b 1–5 mm, T3c 5–15 mm, T3d greater than 15 mm, and this matters prognostically, with a meaningful survival cutoff around T3b (roughly 85% vs. 54% five-year survival on either side of that threshold).

The single most important structure on rectal MRI is the mesorectal fascia (MRF): the fibrous envelope surrounding the rectum and its mesorectum that the surgeon removes en bloc during total mesorectal excision (TME). If tumor, an involved lymph node, or extramural vascular invasion comes within 1 mm of this fascia, the case is called MRF-positive, which predicts a positive circumferential resection margin (CRM) at the time of surgery. This single measurement is what drives the decision to give neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before attempting surgery rather than operating up front.

EMVI (extramural vascular invasion) is a related but distinct finding: serpiginous tumor signal tracking along a vein as it exits the bowel wall into the perirectal fat. It is a marker of hematogenous spread and independently predicts worse prognosis. Nodal staging on MRI, like EMVI assessment, depends on morphology (irregular contour, heterogeneous internal signal) rather than size, up to 40% of nodes smaller than 5 mm still harbor metastatic disease, so a "normal-sized" node cannot be assumed benign. A related staging category, tumor deposits (N1c), refers to discrete irregular foci of tumor along vessels that are separate from the primary tumor and from any identifiable lymph node, and their presence still worsens prognosis and stage.

Anal Cancer, PET-CT for Nodal Staging

Like rectal cancer, nodal assessment in anal cancer on MRI or CT depends on morphology, irregular or spiculated margins, internal necrosis or heterogeneity, because size criteria have not been validated for this disease. What sets anal cancer apart is the outsized value of PET-CT for nodal staging: reported nodal sensitivity is 89–93% for PET-CT versus only around 62% for MRI or CT alone. This is a large enough gap that a PET-CT frequently upstages a patient or reveals a nodal basin that must be added to (or boosted within) the radiation field, which is why guidelines recommend PET-CT especially for T3–T4 or clinically node-positive disease.

T-stage in anal cancer is determined by tumor diameter plus the presence of organ invasion; worth remembering is that direct invasion of the rectal wall or anal sphincter does not, by itself, upstage a tumor to T4: only invasion of other adjacent organs (vagina, urethra, bladder) does. N-stage, as noted in the Workup & Staging section, is defined by nodal location rather than count: inguinal, mesorectal, and internal/external iliac nodes are all regional (N1a/N1b/N1c depending on exact distribution), while para-aortic nodal involvement is classified as distant disease (M1). Current staging uses AJCC 9th edition (2023).

Clinical Pearl Do not rely on PET-CT alone for esophageal T-staging, and do not rely on CT/MRI alone for anal nodal staging, both modalities are excellent at what they're good at (PET for metabolic/nodal activity, cross-sectional imaging for anatomy) but each has a well-documented blind spot that a complementary study (EUS, or PET-CT respectively) is specifically designed to close.
Clinical Pearl The double-duct sign and MRF-positivity are both examples of a single imaging finding directly triggering a treatment pathway, double-duct sign prompts a malignancy workup even before biopsy confirmation, while MRF-positivity is often the deciding factor for whether a rectal cancer patient receives neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy at all.

Treatment Paradigms: Esophageal & Pancre.title: Treatment Paradigms: Esophageal & Pancreatic Cancer
Treatment Paradigms: Esophageal & Pancre.html:
For both esophageal and pancreatic cancer, treatment decisions start with a single gatekeeping question: can this tumor be safely and completely removed with surgery, and if so, should treatment start with surgery or with therapy that shrinks the tumor first? How that question is answered shapes everything that follows.

Esophageal Cancer: Matching Treatment to Depth and Fitness for Surgery

  • T1 tumor, confined to mucosa/submucosa → endoscopic resection (EMR for lesions <1.5cm; ESD for larger lesions, en bloc), ± ablation, preferred over surgery
  • T2–T4 or node-positive, surgical candidate, squamous cell carcinoma → preoperative chemoradiotherapy (41.4–50.4 Gy with concurrent weekly carboplatin/paclitaxel, or capecitabine/5-FU with cisplatin or oxaliplatin) → esophagectomy → adjuvant nivolumab if residual disease (ypT/N+)
  • T2–T4 or node-positive, surgical candidate, adenocarcinoma → either the chemoRT pathway above, or perioperative FLOT (5-FU/leucovorin/oxaliplatin/docetaxel), 4 cycles before and 4 after surgery, without radiation
  • MSI-H/dMMR tumors → neoadjuvant or perioperative immunotherapy alone (e.g., ipilimumab + nivolumab, or pembrolizumab) instead of chemoRT or chemotherapy
  • Not a surgical candidate → definitive chemoradiotherapy, 50.4 Gy/28 fractions with concurrent chemotherapy
  • Cervical esophageal tumors → higher dose, 66–70 Gy (similar to head-and-neck dosing; surgery rarely feasible here)

Squamous cell carcinoma responds so much better to chemoradiation than adenocarcinoma (pathologic complete response roughly doubles) that chemoRT is the natural default for SCC; for adenocarcinoma, both paradigms are legitimate and the choice depends on histology, how obstructive symptoms are (chemoRT relieves dysphagia more reliably), and tolerance for a myelosuppressive regimen like FLOT.

Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma: A Resectability-Driven Algorithm

Pancreatic cancer management is organized around resectability status at diagnosis, not simple TNM stage: ~10–20% present resectable, 10–15% borderline resectable, 30–40% unresectable/locally advanced, and the remainder present with distant metastatic disease.

  • Resectable disease → upfront surgery (Whipple for head tumors; Appleby for body/tail or celiac-axis-involving tumors) → adjuvant chemotherapy (FOLFIRINOX preferred if fit; gemcitabine/capecitabine otherwise)
  • Resectable, positive nodes or positive margins → add adjuvant chemoradiotherapy, 45–50.4 Gy/25–28 fractions with concurrent 5-FU/capecitabine
  • "High-risk resectable" (very high CA 19-9, large primary/bulky nodes, marked weight loss, severe pain) → treat like borderline resectable: neoadjuvant therapy first, even though anatomically resectable now
  • Borderline resectable → neoadjuvant chemotherapy first (FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel; FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/cisplatin if BRCA1/2 or PALB2 mutated), then reassess
  • Borderline resectable, remains borderline after neoadjuvant chemo → add chemoradiotherapy or SBRT before another surgical attempt (goal: reduce R1 resection rate, not shrink the tumor for its own sake)
  • Unresectable/locally advanced → chemotherapy backbone (FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel) ± chemoradiotherapy or SBRT for locoregional control (improves local control, not overall survival); RT alone for symptom palliation
  • SBRT regimen → 33–40 Gy/5 fractions to gross tumor + tumor-vessel interface, 25 Gy/5 fractions to the elective nodal volume (celiac axis, SMA, peripancreatic nodes); 5-fraction strongly preferred over single-fraction (less duodenal/GI toxicity); contraindicated with duodenal perforation
Clinical Pearl In borderline resectable pancreatic cancer, think of radiation's job as "margin insurance," not tumor shrinkage. Its main measured benefit across trials has been a higher rate of clean (R0, margin-negative) resection, the outcome most tightly linked to long-term survival.
Clinical Pearl When an esophageal cancer patient presents with significant obstructive dysphagia, preoperative chemoradiotherapy is often favored over perioperative FLOT chemotherapy alone, since RT more reliably relieves the obstruction while chemotherapy is being delivered.

Treatment Paradigms: Rectal & Anal.title: Treatment Paradigms: Rectal & Anal Cancer
Treatment Paradigms: Rectal & Anal.html:
Both rectal and anal cancer are pelvic malignancies treated with radiation, but they arrived at their modern treatment paradigms from opposite directions. Rectal cancer treatment has spent the last two decades evolving away from mandatory surgery, toward giving more therapy before surgery and, for the right patients, avoiding surgery altogether. Anal cancer, by contrast, has been managed with chemoradiation as the primary curative treatment since the 1970s, with surgery held in reserve for salvage.

Rectal Cancer: From Surgery-Only to Total Neoadjuvant Therapy

  • Stage I (T1–2N0), select small T1 (<3cm, <30% of bowel circumference, margin >3mm, within 8cm of the anal verge, well-to-moderately differentiated, no perineural/lymphovascular invasion) → transanal local excision
  • Stage I, all other patients → total mesorectal excision (TME): low anterior resection (sphincter-sparing) or abdominoperineal resection
  • Low-lying T2 that would otherwise require an APR → chemoradiotherapy first, then restage; a "watch and wait" approach can spare a permanent colostomy
  • Stage II–III (T3–4 or node-positive) → total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT): chemotherapy + chemoradiotherapy before surgery, sequenced either way (induction chemo → chemoRT, or chemoRT → consolidation chemo)
  • T4, node-positive (especially extra-mesorectal), involved mesorectal fascia, low-lying tumor, or planned watch-and-wait → favor long-course chemoRT (45 Gy elective nodal volume, boost to 50.4–54 Gy over ~5–5.5 weeks, concurrent 5-FU or capecitabine)
  • Short-course alternative → 25 Gy/5 fractions, RT alone; more convenient and less immunosuppressive, but less downstaging and less mature watch-and-wait data
  • dMMR/MSI-H tumors → immune checkpoint inhibitor alone (dostarlimab, nivolumab, or pembrolizumab); chemoRT and surgery reserved only for persistent disease at 6 months
  • Complete clinical response after TNT → watch-and-wait surveillance instead of TME

Anal Cancer: Definitive ChemoRT as Primary Therapy

  • Well-differentiated T1N0 anal margin lesion (a discrete skin lesion, clearly separate from the canal) → treated like skin cancer: wide local excision, ≥1cm margin
  • Every other anal cancer (T1N0 in the canal itself, or any T2–T4/node-positive) → definitive chemoradiotherapy is primary curative treatment, not surgery
  • Standard regimen → RT + concurrent 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin-C (2 cycles, weeks 1 and 5)
  • T1–T2N0 → 50.4 Gy/28 fx to the primary, 42 Gy/28 fx to the elective pelvis
  • T3–T4N0 → 54 Gy/30 fx to the primary, 45 Gy/30 fx to the elective pelvis
  • N1 → 54 Gy/30 fx primary + 45 Gy/30 fx pelvis, plus a nodal boost: ≤3cm node to 50.4 Gy/28 fx, >3cm node to 54 Gy/30 fx
  • Assessing treatment response → wait until 26 weeks post-chemoRT; an incomplete response at 11 weeks is common and does not by itself mean treatment failure
  • Truly residual or recurrent disease → salvage abdominoperineal resection (APR)

This approach traces back to the historic "Nigro regimen" at Wayne State, originally designed as preoperative chemoradiotherapy before a mandatory APR; the first patients had such dramatic complete responses that the plan changed to biopsy-only assessment after chemoRT, sparing most patients a permanent colostomy.

Clinical Pearl The rationale for TNT in rectal cancer is threefold, and worth memorizing as a set: better chemotherapy compliance, deeper tumor downstaging, and the chance at organ preservation for complete responders. All three flow from simply moving chemotherapy earlier in the treatment sequence.
Clinical Pearl Never assess anal cancer treatment response before 26 weeks. An incomplete response at the 11-week mark is common and does not, by itself, indicate treatment failure or trigger salvage surgery.

High-Yield Literature.title: High-Yield Literature: GI Cancer Trials
High-Yield Literature.html:
The trials below are the ones that actually changed what oncologists do at the bedside, memorizing their numbers is far less useful than understanding why each one mattered, what question it was really answering, and what came before it that made the result surprising or practice-changing.

Esophageal Cancer

CROSS (van Hagen et al., NEJM 2012) randomized resectable T2–T4 or node-positive esophageal/GEJ cancer to preoperative chemoRT (41.4 Gy/23 fractions with weekly carboplatin/paclitaxel) followed by surgery, versus surgery alone. Median OS was 49 vs. 24 months, and R0 resection rates were 92% vs. 69%, a large enough benefit that this single trial established preoperative chemoRT as a standard paradigm. Notably, pCR rates were much higher for SCC (49%) than adenocarcinoma (23%), a difference that still shapes how oncologists counsel patients about which paradigm to choose today.

CheckMate 577 (Kelly et al., NEJM 2021) addressed the patients CROSS didn't fully solve for: those with residual disease (ypT/N+) after chemoRT and R0 resection. Adjuvant nivolumab for up to one year significantly improved DFS (median 22 vs. 11 months) regardless of histology or PD-L1 status, effectively adding an immunotherapy "backstop" onto the CROSS paradigm for incomplete responders.

ESOPEC (2024 abstracts) directly compared perioperative FLOT chemotherapy to the CROSS chemoRT regimen for esophageal/GEJ adenocarcinoma and found perioperative FLOT significantly improved OS (3-year OS 57% vs. 51%; median OS 66 vs. 37 months) along with better pCR and RFS. This established a genuine second standard-of-care option for adenocarcinoma, though two caveats matter: ESOPEC did not compare against CROSS plus adjuvant nivolumab (the current chemoRT-arm standard), and FLOT is a meaningfully more toxic regimen. The takeaway is that there is no longer a single "right answer" for resectable esophageal/GEJ adenocarcinoma, the choice is individualized by histology, symptom burden (obstruction favors chemoRT), and fitness for a toxic chemotherapy backbone.

Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma

CONKO-001 (Oettle et al., JAMA 2013) and PRODIGE-24 (Conroy et al., NEJM 2018) together established modern adjuvant chemotherapy after pancreatic resection. CONKO-001 showed adjuvant gemcitabine improved OS and DFS over observation; PRODIGE-24 then showed adjuvant modified FOLFIRINOX beat gemcitabine outright (median OS 55 vs. 35 months), making FOLFIRINOX the preferred regimen for fit patients.

ESPAC-1 (Neoptolemos et al., NEJM 2004) deserves special attention not for what it proved, but for the long shadow it cast: using a 2x2 design, it found adjuvant chemotherapy improved OS but adjuvant chemoradiotherapy (delivered with an outdated split-course technique) appeared to worsen OS. This counterintuitive, methodologically flawed result, the trial allowed physicians to choose which arm to randomize patients into, and permitted background treatment outside the assigned arm, created lasting skepticism about the role of radiation in resected pancreatic cancer that persists today, even though later trials like RTOG 0848 have hinted at a DFS benefit in node-negative patients. This is exactly why the role of adjuvant RT in pancreatic cancer remains genuinely unsettled, unlike its role in esophageal or rectal cancer.

PREOPANC-1 (Versteijne et al., JCO 2022) tested neoadjuvant chemoRT (gemcitabine with 36 Gy/15 fractions) against upfront surgery for resectable and borderline resectable disease, and found improved R0 resection (41% vs. 28%) and improved 5-year OS (21% vs. 7%), with the larger benefit concentrated in borderline resectable patients. This helped shift the field's overall thinking toward neoadjuvant strategies, particularly for anything short of straightforwardly resectable disease.

LAP07 (Hammel et al., JAMA 2016) tested adding chemoRT to chemotherapy for unresectable, locally advanced disease and found no OS benefit, but a clear improvement in locoregional control (32% vs. 46% locoregional progression with chemoRT). This trial is what established that radiation's value in unresectable pancreatic cancer is about controlling local/regional disease and its symptoms, not extending survival, which reframes the conversation with patients about the goals of adding RT in this setting.

Rectal Cancer

The Dutch TME trial (Kapiteijn et al., NEJM 2001) tested short-course preoperative RT against surgery alone in the modern era of total mesorectal excision (TME) surgery, and found that even with much-improved surgical technique, RT still reduced local recurrence (5% vs. 11% at 10 years), though without an overall OS benefit except in the stage III, margin-negative subgroup. This established that better surgery reduces, but does not eliminate, the local-control benefit of radiation.

The German CAO/ARO/AIO-94 trial (Sauer et al., NEJM 2004) directly compared preoperative to postoperative chemoRT and found preoperative treatment won on local control (6% vs. 13%) and sphincter preservation (40% vs. 20%), with no OS difference, this established preoperative sequencing as the modern standard. It also revealed that roughly 20% of patients had been clinically overstaged before surgery in the pre-MRI era, a problem substantially reduced now that pelvic MRI is standard.

RAPIDO (Bahadoer et al., Lancet Oncol 2021; updated 2023) is one of the most important cautionary tales in the field. It compared short-course RT plus TNT chemotherapy against long-course chemoRT in higher-risk (T4/node-positive) disease. At 3 years, short-course TNT reduced overall treatment failure, but updated 5-year data showed worse local control with short-course TNT (11.7% vs. 8.1% local recurrence), even though its pCR rate had been higher. The lesson: pCR is not a reliable surrogate for long-term local control, and results from a higher-risk trial population should not be extrapolated to lower-risk patients. Long-course chemoRT remains preferred for T4 tumors, extra-mesorectal nodal disease, an involved MRF, or low-lying tumors.

OPRA (Garcia-Aguilar et al., JCO 2022) and the small dostarlimab study (Cercek et al., NEJM 2022) together represent the most exciting recent direction in rectal cancer. OPRA showed that TNT followed by selective watchful waiting achieves organ preservation in roughly 40–50% of appropriately selected patients, with excellent DFS and OS that match historical surgical controls. The dostarlimab study went further for a specific molecular subgroup: in a phase II trial of only 12 patients with dMMR stage II–III rectal cancer, PD-1 blockade alone produced a 100% sustained complete clinical response, with no patient requiring chemoRT or surgery at follow-up, arguably the single most dramatic result in recent rectal cancer literature, essentially eliminating the need for local therapy in this molecular subgroup.

PROSPECT (Schrag et al., NEJM 2023) tested whether radiation could be omitted entirely for a favorable subset of patients (cT2 node-positive or cT3 N0/+ disease, eligible for sphincter-sparing surgery): neoadjuvant FOLFOX alone, with chemoRT reserved only for an inadequate response, was non-inferior to routine preoperative chemoRT. This is a major de-escalation result, establishing that radiation can be selectively and safely omitted in the right patients rather than being reflexively given to everyone with locally advanced disease.

Anal Cancer

The Nigro regimen (originally reported by Leichman et al., Am J Med 1985, describing the Wayne State protocol) was designed as preoperative chemoRT before a mandatory APR, but the first several patients treated had complete responses, prompting a switch to biopsy-only assessment. This serendipitous finding proved that chemoRT alone could cure anal cancer, transforming it from a disease requiring routine colostomy into one primarily managed medically.

UK ACT I (Northover et al., Br J Cancer 2010) and EORTC 22861 (Bartelink et al., JCO 1997) both confirmed that adding chemotherapy to radiation improved local control and complete response rates compared to RT alone (without an OS difference), cementing chemoRT, not RT alone, as the standard of care.

RTOG 9811 (Ajani et al., JAMA 2008; Gunderson et al., JCO 2012) tested whether induction chemotherapy before chemoRT could improve on straight concurrent 5-FU/mitomycin-C, and found the opposite: concurrent 5-FU/MMC without induction had better 5-year OS (78% vs. 71%) and DFS (68% vs. 58%) than induction plus concurrent 5-FU/cisplatin. This is why 5-FU/mitomycin-C without induction chemotherapy remains the backbone regimen used today.

ACT II (James et al., Lancet Oncol 2013) and its post-hoc analysis (Glynne-Jones et al., Lancet 2017) rounded out the modern regimen: cisplatin showed no PFS advantage over mitomycin-C (so MMC remains preferred for its convenience and toxicity profile), maintenance chemotherapy added no benefit, and, critically, the post-hoc timing analysis showed that many patients without a complete response at 11 weeks went on to respond by 26 weeks. This single finding reshaped surveillance timing across the field, establishing 26 weeks as the point to judge response before considering salvage surgery.

Clinical Pearl RAPIDO is a favorite "trick" trial for a reason: its headline result (short-course TNT reduces treatment failure) is easy to misremember as an unqualified win, but the updated 5-year data showing worse local control is the more clinically important takeaway, and a reminder that pCR and short-term composite endpoints do not always predict long-term local control.
Clinical Pearl The dostarlimab trial in dMMR rectal cancer is one of the highest-yield "future of oncology" data points in this whole curriculum: 12 patients, 100% sustained complete response, zero chemoRT or surgery required. It is a vivid illustration of why universal MSI/MMR testing (see Workup & Staging) matters so much.
